title: Stop building AI agents. Anthropic agrees. Do this.
author: borjafat
content:
KEEP BUILDING AGENTS? Get left behind.

Instead of building many agents for each different job. You need to have a system that allows ONE agent to do all work.

Give your AI a playbook for each recurring job, using these four prompts to write the instructions and reusable files.

![This is how we built Distribb.io to get results like these in SEO. Give it a try.](https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HVE8MjTXoAA1omQ.jpg)

## In this guide

- What you'll get

- Before you begin: where to save the playbook, and who edits its files

- Layer 1: write the steps

- Layer 2: save the tools

## What you'll get

- Why an agent can pass the demo and fail two weeks later

- The three playbook layers: instructions, reusable tools, and checks

- Four ready-to-paste prompts, each with the full instructions it needs

- The files to keep, with completed toolkits for four recurring tasks

- Checks with pass or fail results, so AI finishes the remaining 10 percent

- A folder layout and a complete example showing each week's progress

Set aside about thirty minutes for your first playbook. You can start with an empty folder and use the four prompts below to build it.

You'll also get examples for four recurring jobs and checks to catch unfinished work before it reaches you.

## Why your agents stop working

You've probably heard the advice: build one agent for emails, another for content, and another for leads. Then connect them.

Each one needs its own instructions and tools. When the job changes, you have several places to update, and you usually find the broken connection when you need the result.

Vercel ran into this with its internal data assistant. After months of specialist tools and detailed prompts, the assistant still needed constant maintenance.

The team simplified it to direct file access and basic command-line tools. Its reported success rate rose from 80% to 100%.

Anthropic's skills guide uses a similar idea: give a general agent a folder of instructions and reusable files for each job.

For your own work, start with the decisions you make every week. Write those down so the AI can follow them next time.

## Before you begin: where to save the playbook, and who edits its files

Give each job its own folder. Before you start, check whether your AI can read and edit files in there.

If you're using Claude Code or another agent with file access, create a folder such as ~/playbooks/weekly-client-update. The AI can write SKILL.md there and save the tools it needs.

As you correct its work, have it update those files. Next time, it can read your changes without you explaining them again.

If your chat can only read uploaded Project files, you'll need to save the changes yourself. Ask the AI for the revised file, save it, then replace the Project's old copy.

Typing a correction in the conversation doesn't update the file you uploaded.

Keep the original folder on your computer or in Drive. When the AI revises SKILL.md or a template, save that revision in the folder first.

Then replace the uploaded copy. Remove the old one so the AI doesn't have two versions of the same instructions to choose from.

An upload from Dropbox or Drive is a snapshot, unless your tool explicitly keeps a live connection. If you edit the original, replace the upload too.

Start with a job you do at least weekly. Pick one where you'd spot a bad result immediately and could teach a new hire the basics in under twenty minutes.

Your most repeated task is usually a good place to start. Save the complicated workflow for later.

## Layer 1: write the steps

Have the AI ask you how you do the job. You can explain your choices as you go, including the small ones you'd forget to put in a checklist.

Your SKILL.md should tell the AI when the job applies, what to read, how to do it, and how to check it.

It also needs your decision rules and the problems that have caught you out before. Paste the prompt below into a new chat and let the AI ask the questions.

Prompt to copy

Answer with real examples. If the AI asks something that feels obvious, explain it anyway; the answer may contain a choice you make without thinking.

Expect to correct the first draft. Put those corrections in SKILL.md so the next run uses them.

## Layer 2: save the tools

When the AI makes a script or template you like, save it in the task folder and name it in SKILL.md. Otherwise, you may pay it to build the same thing again next week and get a slightly different version.

Anthropic's skills guide recommends keeping reusable scripts alongside the instructions so Claude can run code it already has.

Files worth keeping in the toolbox:

- Scripts for repeatable operations, such as fetching figures, changing filenames, or converting file types.

- Templates with square-bracket placeholders that keep the layout consistent while you change the details.

- Reference files containing correct client spellings, products, prices, URLs, and account identifiers.

- Completed examples you approved, so the AI can see the tone you want in actual work.

- Written rules for your voice, document formatting, and vocabulary you want it to avoid.

- Prompts for smaller actions you repeat regularly.

Keep the files you'd hand a new hire on day one. Leave out one-time outputs, unfinished drafts, and anything with passwords or API keys.

Run the job once with the AI. When a piece works, ask it to replace your details with placeholders and save a reusable copy.

On the second run, watch what it builds again. Those repeated pieces tell you what to add to the folder next.

Prompt to copy

Examples of a finished toolbox:

Weekly client reports: a numbers-pull script, update-template.md, two updates the client liked, client-names.md containing approved spellings, and tone-rules.md.

Repurposing content: hook-bank.md, caption-template.md, brand-voice.md, and three successful posts with a short explanation of what worked.

Following up on invoices: three emails for different overdue stages, escalation-ladder.md, account-contacts.md, and tone-rules.md to keep day-sixty messages friendly.

Screening applicants: scorecard.md, role-brief.md, five sample responses with ratings, and rejection-email.md.

Once a month, remove unused files and keep one version for each purpose. Two similar templates can leave the AI guessing which one you want.

## Layer 3: test the work

Write down what the finished work has to pass. Then have the AI run those checks and show you the evidence before you review it.

That way, you can review the result without rechecking every detail yourself.

Anthropic found that agents sometimes marked features complete before testing the whole user flow. Check what the finished work actually does.

Match figures and claims to their sources, open links, check names against your reference file, or count the words.

For a visual output, inspect a screenshot of the finished result. For code, run the test. Every check needs a condition that would make it fail.

Prompt to copy

Examples of useful checks for each task:

Weekly client reports: every number matches the exported data, descriptive claims include a supporting figure, fewer than 200 words, client spelling matches client-names.md, and the action promised in the previous update is addressed.

Repurposing content: fewer than 12 words in the hook, no terms prohibited by brand-voice.md, claims agree with the original transcript, and the caption's opening doesn't reveal the payoff.

Invoice follow-ups: the balance agrees with the invoice, the due date matches, the email follows the approved template for that overdue stage, and the payment URL loads.

Applicant screening: each rating includes a quotation from the response, every score has supporting evidence, and the summary agrees with the interview transcript.

## The loop: save corrections in the playbook

When the AI gets something wrong, save the correction in the task folder. A fix left in the conversation may be missing when you start a new chat next week.

Update the file that future runs will read, then rerun the job to see whether the fix holds.

Ask which layer caused the mistake. Add a missing step or decision rule to the instructions.

If it rebuilt a file you already had, or used an outdated one, fix the toolbox. If a check should have caught the error, update the completion checks.

Change the file responsible for the problem so you don't have to rewrite the whole playbook.

Prompt to copy

Read notes.md once a month. If the same step keeps going wrong, that's a good candidate for a dedicated script or another tool that can do it reliably.

## The folder after you set it up

Folder layout

Keep a separate folder for each job. If the AI confuses two tasks, check the When to use this descriptions in their SKILL.md files.

Use the phrases you'd actually type when asking for each job. That gives the AI a specific reason to choose the right playbook.

## A complete example: sending the weekly client update

Suppose you're handing over the weekly client update. During the interview, you explain that you export last week's ad figures, compare them with the targets, and explain what changed.

You also mention that you always open with the figure that moved most and keep the tone brief and honest.

That opening rule is easy to leave out of a checklist. It's also something you'd notice straight away if the AI wrote the update without it.

After the first run, save the data-pull script and the update template you liked.

In week two, add an update the client responded well to. Keep the correct client spellings and agreed targets in a reference file.

Set five checks: every figure matches the export, descriptive claims include numbers, the update stays under 200 words, the client name is correct, and last week's promised action is addressed.

Suppose an invented figure slips through in week four. Tighten the data check so every number needs an exact source match, record the fix, and rerun the update.

By week six, the aim is to review and send a report the AI has already checked.

## Five errors to prevent

- Documenting everything from memory. Let the interview draw out your decisions, and answer the obvious questions that reveal choices you normally make without thinking about them.

- One folder holding every task. The AI has to guess which job's instructions you wanted.

- Using vague triggers. A description like help with content doesn't identify a particular task. Write the phrases you'd use when asking for that exact result.

- Skipping the checks. You still have to inspect every detail, which is work you meant to hand over.

- Corrections left in chat. If you don't save the change in the folder, expect to repeat it next week.

## Your first half hour

Pick your most frequent task and start with prompt one. Spend around fifteen minutes answering the interview with real examples.

Run the job once, then use prompt two to save the pieces that worked. Add the checks with prompt three.

Repeat the task once more, and see which parts you no longer have to explain.
